TL;DR Summary: I have a question about a simple mathematical model.

I have a question about a simple mathematical model. I am not looking for an answer, just a hint as to what I am doing wrong.
Consider a population of size N. We can assume N is large, and that everyone in the population is susceptible to a disease. We also assume that the disease is viral, and that the virus is transmitted through contact with an infected person. We assume that the rate of contact between individuals is proportional to the number of people in the population. This is the infection rate, and we call it ##\beta##. We assume that the rate at which infected people recover is ##\gamma##. We assume that the disease is not fatal, and that recovered people are immune for life.
We want to model the number of infected people, ##I(t)##, as a function of time. We can do this by considering the rate of change of ##I(t)##. The rate of change of ##I(t)## is the number of people who get infected, minus the number of people who recover. The number of people who get infected is proportional to the number of infected people, and the number of people in the population. The number of people who recover is proportional to the number of infected people. This gives us the differential equation:
$$\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta I (N - I) - \gamma I$$
We can simplify this to:
$$\frac{dI}{dt} = (\beta N - (\beta + \gamma))I - \beta I^2$$

Covid-19 and asymptomatic transmission: a systematic review of the literature.

The COVID-19 pandemic has spread rapidly across the globe, with Africa being the last continent to report locally transmitted cases. The true extent of community transmission in Africa is unknown, but asymptomatic or paucisymptomatic cases may have played a role in the spread of the disease. This review aimed to determine the prevalence of asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection in Africa and the contribution of asymptomatic individuals to disease transmission. A literature search was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar using the keywords "SARS-CoV-2," "COVID-19," "asymptomatic," "paucisymptomatic," "prevalence," and "Africa." A total of 15 articles were selected for the review. The prevalence of asymptomatic COVID-19 ranged from 12% to 40% in all studies. The majority of asymptomatic cases were younger and not hospitalized. Asymptomatic individuals had viral loads similar to symptomatic cases. The Zambian researchers also stressed that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases seemed to be more common in Africa at the time. Asymptomatic or paucisymptomatic cases may have contributed to the spread of COVID-19 in Africa. There is a need for large-scale genomic surveillance in Africa to determine the extent of community transmission and the contribution of asymptomatic cases to disease spread.

samples.hyp:
Abstract
Polygenic scores (PGS) are increasingly used in biomedical research and have been proposed as a means to improve health care. However, most PGS have been developed in and calibrated against European populations, which may limit their generalizability to other populations. In particular, the generalizability of PGS to sub-Saharan African populations has not been well studied. Here, we investigate the generalizability of PGS across diverse populations in West Africa using data from the 1,000 Genomes Project. We find that the performance of PGS declines substantially when applied to populations from different super-populations, including sub-Saharan African populations. This loss of performance is not fully explained by differences in individual ancestry or environmental factors. These results suggest that the low performance of PGS in non-European populations is due to a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors. We also find that PGS are more generalizable within Europe than between European and non-European populations. Our results highlight the importance of developing PGS in diverse global populations to improve their utility in health care and other applications.

samples.src: This study evaluated visual and cytology screening in preventing cervical intraepithelial lesions (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
samples.ref: Wannan binciken ya kimanta binciken gani da cytology a cikin hana cututtukan intraepithelial na mahaifa (CIN) da kuma kansar mahaifa a ƙasar Namibiya.
samples.hyp:
Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in women worldwide. In Namibia, cervical cancer is the most common cancer in women. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of visual screening and cytology screening in preventing CIN and cervical cancer in Namibia. The study was a retrospective cohort study of women who attended the Gynecology Clinic at the Windhoek Central Hospital between 1992 and 2002. The women were divided into three groups: Group 1 had visual screening only, Group 2 had cytology screening only, and Group 3 had both visual and cytology screening. The incidence of CIN and cervical cancer was compared between the three groups. The results showed that the incidence of CIN and cervical cancer was significantly lower in Group 3 than in Group 1 and Group 2. The study concluded that both visual and cytology screening are effective in preventing CIN and cervical cancer in Namibia. The study also recommended that all women in Namibia should be screened for cervical cancer.

Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, with more than 500,000 new cases diagnosed each year. In the United States, more than 12,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer each year, and more than 4,000 women die from the disease each year. Worldwide, more than 270,000 women die from cervical cancer each year. Cervical cancer is caused by a virus called human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is a very common virus that is passed from one person to another through sexual contact. Most people who become infected with HPV do not develop cervical cancer. However, some types of HPV can cause changes in the cells of the cervix that can lead to cervical cancer. Cervical cancer can be prevented by getting vaccinated against HPV and by having regular Pap tests. Cervical cancer can be treated with surgery, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy. The earlier cervical cancer is found and treated, the better the chance of a cure.

samples.ref: Ƙaddamar da maƙasudin ƙasa-da-ƙasa don kawar da ciwon hanta na B (HBV), mun tashi don kwatanta ɗaiɗaikun mutane tare da kamuwa HBV da kuma waɗanda suka kamu da cututtuka biyu, wato HBVB/HIV, don kimanta tasirin jiyya da kuma jagoranci ingantawa a cikin kulawar asibiti.
samples.hyp:
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa. The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of HBV infection and identify the associated risk factors in pregnant women attending antenatal clinic at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Enugu, Nigeria. 1000 pregnant women were recruited for the study. Blood samples were collected and tested for HBsAg, HBcAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, HBV DNA, CD4 count and HIV antibodies. The data were analysed using SPSS version 16.0. The prevalence of HBV infection was 10.6% (106/1000). 67.9% of the HBsAg positive women were HBeAg positive. 8.5% of the women had low CD4 count (<350 cells/μl). 1.1% of the women were coinfected with HBV and HIV. The majority of the HIV positive women (66.7%) were on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). There was no significant association between CD4 count and seroconversion from HBeAg to HBeAb (p=0.074). The level of HBV DNA was significantly lower in the women who were on HAART (p<0.001). The level of HBV DNA was significantly higher in the women who were HBeAg positive (p<0.001). The level of HBV DNA was significantly lower in the women who had seroconverted from HBeAg to HBeAb (p<0.001). The prevalence of hepatitis B virus infection in this study was high. There is a need for routine screening of pregnant women for hepatitis B virus infection and for the follow-up of infected women to prevent mother-to-child transmission. The level of viraemia was significantly lower in HIV/HBV coinfected women who were on HAART. 1Background
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa.2 It is estimated that 80–90% of those chronically infected at birth acquire chronic hepatitis, 20–30% cirrhosis and 15–25% hepatocellular carcinoma by the fifth decade of life.3 The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 350 million people are chronically infected

Researchers give guidelines to improve hepatitis B treatment

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major global health problem, with 240 million chronically infected people worldwide and 600,000 to 1.2 million deaths per year from HBV-related liver disease. The natural history of chronic HBV infection is highly variable, and treatment decisions are further complicated by the lack of a highly predictive assay for HBeAg seroconversion using pegylated interferon alfa (PEG-IFNα).

A new review published in The Lancet by a distinguished group of HBV experts provides recommendations for the management of patients with chronic HBV infection. The authors discuss the many challenges in treating chronic HBV, including the natural history of the disease, the lack of predictive assays, and the lack of long-term efficacy and safety data for many of the drugs used in clinical practice.

The review begins with an overview of the natural history of chronic HBV infection, which is highly variable and can be difficult to predict. The authors note that treatment decisions are further complicated by the lack of a highly predictive assay for HBeAg seroconversion using PEG-IFNα. They go on to discuss the many challenges in treating chronic HBV, including the lack of long-term efficacy and safety data for many of the drugs used in clinical practice.

The authors provide recommendations for the management of patients with chronic HBV infection, including the use of antiviral therapy for patients with high viral loads and low CD4+ T-cell counts. They also recommend regular monitoring of patients for liver function and other potential complications of chronic HBV infection.

The review concludes by emphasizing the need for continued research into the treatment of chronic HBV infection. The authors note that while significant progress has been made in the development of new therapies, there is still much to be learned about the natural history of the disease and the best ways to treat it.

Overall, this review provides valuable insights into the challenges of treating chronic HBV infection and offers recommendations for improving patient outcomes. As research in this area continues, it is hoped that new therapies will be developed that are more effective and have fewer side effects than current treatments.

In a recent study, researchers were able to highlight how being infected with both hepatitis B (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may offer a treatment advantage over infection with only HBV.
The study, “Telaprevir is efficacious in hepatitis B virus (HBV)-infected HIV-infected individuals with HBV/HIV dual suppression and HBV resistance to telaprevir,” was published in the journal Antiviral Therapy.
The research was led by first author Dr. David L. Paton, of the University of California, San Diego, and his colleagues.
Telaprevir is an antiviral drug that is used to treat chronic hepatitis C infection. It is not approved to treat hepatitis B, but researchers are interested in its potential use in this population.
The study was designed to evaluate the effect of telaprevir in people with chronic hepatitis B who were also infected with HIV, and who had previously been treated with pegylated interferon and ribavirin, but did not respond to this therapy.
The researchers found that 10 of the 14 participants (71%) had a reduction in HBV DNA levels after treatment with telaprevir, and five of the 10 (50%) had a reduction in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels. In addition, three of the 14 participants (21%) experienced a loss of HBsAg.
These results suggest that telaprevir may be effective in treating hepatitis B in people who are also infected with HIV, but more research is needed to confirm these findings.
The study was limited by its small sample size, and the participants were all receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV, which may have affected the results. In addition, the study was not designed to compare the effectiveness of telaprevir to other treatments for hepatitis B.
Overall, the study provides some promising results for the use of telaprevir in treating hepatitis B in people who are also infected with HIV, but more research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal treatment approach for this population.

HIV-1-specific CD8+ T cells from elite controllers and chronically infected patients receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) have similar polyfunctionality and specificity, but different immunodominance hierarchies.
PLoS Pathog 16 (10): e1008822 (2020-10-01)PMID 33006395
HIV-1-specific CD8(+) T cell responses are weaker in elite controllers (ECs) than in progressors, but the former control viral replication without antiretroviral therapy (ART). We compared the T cell responses of EC controllers and controllers on ART (ARTCs) with those of progressors on ART (ARTP). Ex vivo, HIV-1-specific CD8(+) T cell responses were weaker in ARTC and EC compared to ARTP, but ART-induced exhaustion was excluded as the cause. During proliferation, ARTC and ARTP cells showed similar expression of HLA-DR and CD38, but EC cells showed lower expression. The frequency of cells producing cytokines and cytotoxic molecules was lower in ARTC and EC than in ARTP, but the polyfunctionality was similar. The specificity of the responses was also similar between ARTC and EC, but EC responses showed higher frequencies of cells recognizing peptides from HIV-1 proteins that were not included in the assays. The immunodominance hierarchies differed between ARTC and EC, but not between ARTC and ARTP. Our data suggest that the magnitude of the T cell response is reduced in EC and ARTC, but that the polyfunctionality, specificity, and quality of the response are largely maintained.

Business women in Niger need more security
A woman sells her products in the streets of Niamey, Niger. (Photo: AFP)

Business women in Niger are calling for more security in the country, as they are often the target of robberies and attacks, the head of the National Association of Women Entrepreneurs (ANETI) said on Monday.

“Security is a major problem for women entrepreneurs in Niger. They are often the target of robberies and attacks,” said Halima Mamane, president of ANETI.

She made the remarks during a meeting with the head of the National Gendarmerie, Colonel Abdoulaye Issa, who is currently touring the country to meet with security chiefs.

Mamane said that women entrepreneurs are often forced to close their businesses due to insecurity, which is a major obstacle to their development.

“We are calling on the authorities to take measures to ensure the security of women entrepreneurs,” she said.

Colonel Issa said that the security situation in the country is improving, and that the National Gendarmerie is working to ensure the security of all Nigeriens.

He said that the National Gendarmerie is aware of the problems faced by women entrepreneurs, and is working to find solutions.

“We are aware of the problems faced by women entrepreneurs, and we are working to find solutions,” he said.

The meeting between the two parties was a success, and both parties agreed to continue working together to improve the security situation in the country.

“We are committed to working together to improve the security situation in the country,” said Mamane.

The meeting was held at the headquarters of the National Gendarmerie in Niamey, the capital of Niger.

The National Association of Women Entrepreneurs (ANETI) was founded in 2015, and is made up of women entrepreneurs from all over the country.

The association is working to promote the development of women entrepreneurs in Niger, and to improve their access to finance and markets.

The National Gendarmerie is the main security force in Niger, and is responsible for maintaining law and order in the country.

The gendarmerie is currently working to improve its relations with the civilian population, and to increase its presence in rural areas.

The meeting between ANETI and the National Gendarmerie was a positive step in the right direction, and both parties are committed to continuing their work together to improve the security situation in the country.

Background
Preterm birth is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. The aetiology of preterm birth is complex and multifactorial. The role of oxidative stress in preterm birth has been suggested. Background: The occurrence of preterm birth (PTB) is a major public health problem worldwide. The etiology of preterm birth is complex and multifactorial. The identification of additional risk factors may help to further elucidate the pathophysiology of preterm birth. Nutritional status of the mother is a potential risk factor for preterm birth. The objective of this study was to assess the use of hair element concentrations as biomarkers for nutritional status and their association with preterm birth.
Methods: A total of 103 women who delivered at the University Hospital of North Norway were included in this study. Women were divided into two groups: term delivery (n = 75; 39-41 gestational weeks) and preterm delivery (n = 28; <37 gestational weeks). Hair samples (10 cm) were collected from all participants. Trace elements (Cu, Zn, Pb, and Hg) were analyzed in hair samples by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The concentrations of Cu and Zn in maternal hair samples were log-transformed and compared between the two delivery groups by unpaired t-test. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for preterm birth were calculated based on median hair element concentrations in the two delivery groups. English:
For this study, researchers aimed to measure the amounts of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who had preterm births, and then to determine the odds that preterm birth is caused by high amounts of each of the micronutrients studied.

Materials and methods
The study was conducted using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2009–2014. The NHANES is a nationally representative survey of the civilian, non-institutionalized population of the United States. The survey is conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The NHANES is a cross-sectional survey that combines interviews and physical examinations. The NHANES Institutional Review Board (IRB) has approved all protocols. The NCHS has also determined that the NHANES does not require informed consent because the data are collected in a surveillance context and do not contain any information that would lead to the identification of study participants. The NCHS website provides full information on the NHANES survey design, data collection, and protocols. The data used in this study were obtained from the NHANES website (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/index.htm).

The study population included 20,565 women of reproductive age (18–44 years) who had given birth in the previous 12 months. The outcome of interest was preterm birth, defined as birth at <37 weeks of gestation. The exposure of interest was the concentration of selenium, copper, and zinc in maternal serum. The concentrations of these elements were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) on serum samples collected during the interview examination cycle. The ICP-MS is a highly sensitive and accurate method for measuring trace elements in biological samples. The details of the laboratory methods used to measure the element concentrations are provided on the NHANES website (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nhanes/nhanes2013-2014/ACRDP_ACRES_Analysis_Notes.aspx).

The odds of preterm birth associated with high concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were estimated using multivariable logistic regression models. samples.src: HIV-positive participants with tuberculous meningitis were recruited from South African hospitals and randomized to one of three rifampicin dosing groups:
samples.ref: An ɗauki mahalarta masu cutar HIV masu fama da cutar sanƙarau na ƙwaƙwalwa daga asibitocin Afirka ta Kudu kuma an ba su bazuwar zuwa ɗaya daga cikin rukunonin adadin rifampicin guda uku:
samples.hyp:
1. 10 mg/kg once daily for 14 days,
2. 20 mg/kg once daily for 7 days, or
3. 20 mg/kg once daily for 14 days.

The primary outcome was mortality at 90 days.

What the researchers found

Of the 120 patients included in the trial, 40 were assigned to each arm.

The mortality rate at 90 days was significantly lower in the two higher dose groups than in the low dose group (10 mg/kg for 14 days vs. 20 mg/kg for 7 days or 14 days: 25% vs. 40% or 35%; p=0.049).

The treatment was generally well tolerated, with no cases of rashes or alanine aminotransferase elevations.

Why this study is important

These results suggest that lower rifampicin doses can be safely used to treat tuberculous meningitis in HIV-positive adults.

Lower doses may be particularly important in patients with severe renal or hepatic impairment, as these patients are at increased risk of rifampicin-associated rash and alanine aminotransferase elevations.

This study was limited by its small sample size and the fact that the investigators did not perform lumbar punctures on all patients, which could have led to an underestimation of the efficacy of the lower dose regimens.

What this means for patients

These results suggest that HIV-positive patients with tuberculous meningitis can be treated with a lower rifampicin dose than is currently recommended, which may reduce the risk of adverse effects.

Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops

Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops

Soil quality is a term used to describe the ability of the soil to support crops. The quality of the soil is determined by its physical, chemical and biological properties. The physical properties of the soil are its texture, structure, porosity and density. The chemical properties of the soil are its pH, nutrient content, cation exchange capacity and salinity. The biological properties of the soil are its organic matter content, microbial activity, earthworm population and other soil organisms.

The quality of the soil is important for the growth and development of crops. Poor soil quality can lead to low crop yields, poor crop quality and increased susceptibility to pests and diseases. Therefore, it is important to improve the quality of the soil in order to increase crop productivity and sustainability.

One way to improve the quality of the soil is by adding biochar and compost. Biochar is a type of charcoal that is produced by heating organic material in the absence of oxygen. Compost is a mixture of decomposed organic material that is used as a soil amendment. Both biochar and compost have been shown to improve the physical, chemical and biological properties of the soil.

The physical properties of the soil can be improved by adding biochar and compost. Biochar has a high porosity and surface area, which can increase the water-holding capacity of the soil. Compost can also improve the soil structure by increasing the aggregation of soil particles. This can improve the aeration and drainage of the soil, which is important for the growth of crops.

The chemical properties of the soil can also be improved by adding biochar and compost. Biochar has a high cation exchange capacity, which can increase the nutrient-holding capacity of the soil. Compost can also increase the nutrient content of the soil by adding organic matter and nutrients. This can improve the availability of nutrients to crops, which is important for their growth and development.

The biological properties of the soil can also be improved by adding biochar and compost. Biochar can provide a habitat for soil microorganisms, which can increase microbial activity in the soil. samples.hyp:
The Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network in Rheumatoid Arthritis and its Relation to Autoimmunity, Inflammation and Thrombosis
The Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network in Rheumatoid Arthritis and its Relation to Autoimmunity, Inflammation and Thrombosis

The fibrin network is a key component of the blood clot. It is formed by the polymerization of fibrinogen into fibrin monomers, which subsequently form fibrin dimers that are cross-linked by factor XIIIa to form a fibrinogen network. The structure of the fibrin network is of importance for the function of the blood clot, and thus for hemostasis and thrombosis. The aim of this thesis was to study the fibrin network in plasma from patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and to study the relation between the structure of the fibrin network and autoimmunity, inflammation and thrombosis in these patients. The main findings were that the fibrin network in RA is atypical, and that the atypical network structure is related to autoantibodies to citrullinated vimentin and factor XIIIa, and to an increased risk of venous thrombosis. The atypical network structure was characterized by a low number of branches per fiber, a low number of fiber cross-links and a high number of fiber knots. The atypical network structure was found in plasma from patients with RA, patients with other autoimmune diseases, and healthy elderly persons, but not in plasma from healthy young persons. Thus, an atypical fibrin network structure seems to be a feature of autoimmunity in general, and not specific for RA. The atypical network structure was not related to markers of inflammation, which indicates that the atypical network structure is not secondary to inflammation. The atypical network structure was, however, related to autoantibodies to citrullinated vimentin, which indicates that autoantibodies may be involved in the formation of the atypical network structure. The atypical network structure was also related to an increased risk of venous thrombosis, which indicates that the atypical network structure may be a risk marker for venous thrombosis. In conclusion, the fibrin network in RA is atypical, and the atypical network structure seems to be related to autoimmunity and thrombosis in these patients.

samples.ref: Dungulewar jinni cikin masu ciwon gavvai manuniya ce kan yanda suke iya kamuwa da bugun zuciya da garsa.
samples.hyp:
Blood clotting in arthritis patients may explain their increased risk for heart attack, stroke
Blood clots are a common occurrence in people with rheumatoid arthritis, and a new study suggests that the clots may help explain the increased risk of heart attack and stroke in these patients.
Blood clots are a common occurrence in people with rheumatoid arthritis, and a new study suggests that the clots may help explain the increased risk of heart attack and stroke in these patients. (Shutter)
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease that primarily affects joints, but it also increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events like heart attack and stroke.
Compared with people without RA, patients with the condition have a 50 percent increased risk of cardiovascular disease and are twice as likely to have a heart attack or stroke, according to background information in the study.
The reasons for this increased risk are not fully understood, but inflammation and damage to blood vessels from RA may play a role. Some studies have also suggested that RA medications may increase the risk of blood clots, which can lead to heart attack and stroke.
To better understand the role of blood clots in the increased risk of cardiovascular disease in RA, the researchers enrolled 113 patients with the condition and 98 people without it.
The researchers took blood samples from each participant and put them in a machine that makes blood clot. They found that the blood of RA patients took less than half the time to clot compared with the blood of people without RA.
They also found that the more severe the RA, the faster the blood clotted. The researchers say that these findings suggest that people with RA are prone to developing blood clots.

The team obtained blood samples from 126 people with rheumatoid arthritis and 96 healthy volunteers. They found that people with rheumatoid arthritis had increased numbers of neutrophils and that these neutrophils had altered the proteins on their surface. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, was led by researchers at the University of Illinois at Chicago and the Jesse Brown VA Medical Center.
The researchers examined blood clots from 12 patients who had died of sepsis, a severe and often fatal reaction to infection, and 12 patients who had died of non-septic causes.
Sepsis causes widespread inflammation throughout the body, which can damage blood vessels and make them more likely to clot.
The researchers found that fibrins in blood clots from sepsis patients had different properties than fibrins in clots from patients who died of other causes.
The fibrins in sepsis clots were more resistant to being broken down, and had a more open, porous structure.
The study suggests that the structural changes in fibrins may make them more likely to trap inflammatory cells and other components of the immune system, which could contribute to the tissue damage seen in sepsis.
“Fibrin is a major component of blood clots, and it’s well known that inflammation plays a role in sepsis,” said study co-author Patricia Janicki, professor and chair of the department of pharmacology at the UIC College of Medicine.
“But the exact contribution of fibrin to sepsis has been unclear. Our findings suggest that fibrin may play a more prominent role than previously thought.”
The researchers are now working on developing tests to detect the structural changes in fibrin that they found in the sepsis clots.
Such a test could help doctors identify patients who are at high risk of developing severe sepsis, and may eventually lead to new treatments that target fibrin to improve outcomes for sepsis patients.
“Right now, we don’t have any good treatments for sepsis,” Janicki said.
“Our hope is that by better understanding the role of fibrin in sepsis, we can develop new therapies that could make a real difference for patients.”

Marine meteorological forecasts for coastal ocean users – perceptions, usability and uptake
Marine meteorological forecasts are a critical input to safe and efficient operation of a range of activities in the coastal ocean. These forecasts are produced by a range of providers, including the South African Weather Service, which produces a number of marine products, and the South African National Biodiversity Institute, which produces a monthly marine forecast for the False Bay area. In this article, we report on a study that investigated perceptions of marine forecasts, their usability, and uptake by a range of users of the False Bay marine forecast. The study used a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, including a survey of users, interviews, and focus group discussions. The results indicate that users generally have a positive perception of the marine forecast, and find it useful for their activities. However, there are some areas where the forecast could be improved, such as providing more detailed information on wave height and direction, and improving the clarity of the language used. The study also found that there are some barriers to uptake of the forecast, such as lack of awareness of the forecast, and difficulty in accessing the forecast. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the needs and preferences of users of marine forecasts, which can inform the development of more effective and user-friendly forecasts.

samples.src: An evidence based surgical algorithm for management of Odontogenic keratocyst
samples.ref: Hanyoyi ɗin tiyata na shaida domin kulawa da Raunin muƙamuƙi
samples.hyp:
An evidence based surgical algorithm for management of Odontogenic keratocyst
Hassan A. El-Awady, MD, MSc, M. El-Zoghbi, MD, MSc, and A. El-Zoghbi, BSc
Abstract
Introduction: Odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is a challenging lesion with a high recurrence rate. The aim of this study was to develop an evidence based surgical algorithm for management of OKC.
Methods: Literature search was performed using the following databases: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. The search was conducted using the keywords: odontogenic keratocyst, management, treatment, and recurrence. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for nonrandomized studies. The quality of the evidence and the grade of recommendation were assessed using the GRADEpro® Guidelines.
Results: A total of 1544 articles were retrieved, and 24 articles were selected for full-text review. Among the 24 articles, 12 were included in the methodological quality assessment. The OKC management options were classified as low, moderate, or high quality of evidence. A strong recommendation was made to enucleation followed by adjunctive treatment. A moderate recommendation was made for marsupialization as a first-line treatment option. While the evidence for recurrence prevention was of low quality, a strong recommendation was made against routine marginal resection.
Conclusions: This study provides an evidence-based surgical algorithm for the management of OKC. Further research is needed to investigate the effectiveness of different management options and to identify the optimal treatment approach for different cases.
Keywords: Odontogenic keratocyst, Management, Treatment, Recurrence

Poor point-of-care testing in South Africa and India delays healthcare
10/10/2019
By
Sara Reardon
, Nature
South Africa
and
India
are among the countries with the worst point-of-care testing, according to a new study.
The study, published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering1, found that 10 countries — including South Africa, India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo — have no point-of-care tests available for more than 50% of the diseases for which the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends them.
Point-of-care tests are designed to be used outside of a laboratory, often in low-resource settings. They are typically small, easy to use and can provide results in minutes. The tests are particularly useful in remote areas, where patients may have to travel long distances to reach a hospital or clinic.
The WHO recommends point-of-care tests for 67 diseases, including HIV, malaria, tuberculosis and Ebola. The tests are intended to help health-care providers make decisions about treatment and to help patients access care more quickly.
The new study found that South Africa and India have the worst point-of-care testing coverage. In South Africa, only 1% of the diseases for which the WHO recommends point-of-care tests have any tests available. In India, the figure is 2%.
The study also found that 15 countries — including the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand — have excellent point-of-care testing coverage. In these countries, more than 90% of the diseases for which the WHO recommends point-of-care tests have at least one test available.
The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Oxford, the University of Washington and the University of California, San Francisco. The researchers analyzed data from the WHO and from other sources to create a global map of point-of-care testing coverage.
The study highlights the need for more investment in point-of-care testing, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Point-of-care tests can help to improve health-care delivery and to save lives.

samples.src: Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis
samples.ref: Zuwa ga ma'anar rashin lafiya mai tsanani da kulawa mai mahimmanci ta amfani da nazarin ra'ayi
samples.hyp:
Go to ...
Go to ...


Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis

Critical Care volume 25, Article number: 101 (2021) Cite this article
Metrics details
Critical illness and critical care are widely used terms in critical care practice, research, and policy. However, the terms are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This can lead to confusion and misinterpretation of data. This paper reports on a concept analysis of critical illness and critical care to clarify the terms and provide a foundation for future research.
Walker and Avant (2015) were used to analyse critical illness and critical care.
Searches of CINAHL, PubMed, and PsycINFO identified 13 papers for critical illness and 21 papers for critical care that met the criteria for primary data. Braun and Clarke’s (2006) method of thematic analysis was used to analyse the data.
Critical illness is a state of severe physiological derangement that is life-threatening and requires urgent, expert medical intervention. Critical care is the specialised health care provided to patients with critical illness.
Definitions of critical illness and critical care were clarified. This provides a foundation for future research and the development of theory. The definitions can also be used to inform policy and practice. Further research is required to explore the use of the definitions in these areas.

The study has several strengths. First, it is the first study to examine the association between the COVID-19 pandemic and the incidence of acute myocardial infarction in a real-world setting. Second, the study used a large sample size and a long follow-up period. Third, the study used a well-established and validated administrative database. Finally, the study adjusted for several potential confounding factors, including age, sex, comorbidities, and medication use.
The study also has several limitations. First, it is an observational study, and therefore, it cannot establish causality. Second, the study used administrative data, which may not be as accurate as data collected through clinical trials. Third, the study did not have information on some potential confounding factors, such as socioeconomic status and lifestyle factors. Finally, the study was conducted in a single country, and therefore, the results may not be generalizable to other countries.
Conclusion
The study found that the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a significant increase in the incidence of acute myocardial infarction in a real-world setting. The study also found that the increase in incidence was more pronounced in men and in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. The study highlights the need for further research to understand the mechanisms underlying the association between the COVID-19 pandemic and acute myocardial infarction.

samples.src: In this study researchers identified specific genes that play a role in malaria infections in liver cells, which could lead to new anti-malaria drug targets in future.
samples.ref: A cikin wannan binciken, masu bincike sun gano takamaiman qwayoyin halittar da ke taka rawa wajen kamuwa da cutar zazzavin cizon sauro a cikin qwayoyin hanta, wanda zai iya haifar da sabbin dabarun yaqi da zazzavin cizon sauro nan gaba.
samples.hyp:
In this study researchers identified specific genes that play a role in malaria infections in liver cells, which could lead to new anti-malaria drug targets in future.
Malaria is a disease caused by a parasite that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. The parasite travels to the liver, where it infects liver cells. The infection can then spread to the blood and cause symptoms such as fever and chills.
The researchers in this study used a technique called CRISPR/Cas9 to edit the genes of liver cells and see which ones were important for the parasite to infect the cells. They identified several genes that were involved in the infection process, and further experiments showed that blocking these genes could prevent the parasite from infecting the cells.
These findings could lead to the development of new drugs that target these specific genes, potentially providing new treatments for malaria. However, more research is needed to fully understand the role of these genes in the infection process and to develop safe and effective drugs.
Source: Science Daily

The “knocked out” cells were genetically engineered to lack a protein called OAS1. People with two copies of a specific version of this gene are better able to fight off infections.

The researchers found that when the liver cells had the OAS1 protein, the parasites were less able to multiply and infect red blood cells. The infected red blood cells were less able to stick to the lining of blood vessels, which is what causes the symptoms of malaria.

The researchers also found that the malaria parasites were more likely to die when they were inside the “knocked out” liver cells.

The researchers don’t yet know how the OAS1 protein helps the immune system fight malaria. They suspect that it may somehow interfere with the ability of the malaria parasite to multiply.

The study was published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort
Bekker, T.M. and Richardson, D.M. and Rejmankova, E. and Joubert, Z. and Mucina, L. and Moller, A. and Moller, J. and Mouton, M. and New, T.R. and Reyers, B. and Roux, J. and van Wilgen, B. and Wilson, B. (2008) Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort. In: Van Wilgen, B.W. and Thomas, D.A. and Bond, W.J. and van Oosterhout, C.A.M. and Cowling, R.M., (eds.) South African Perspectives on Terrestrial Global Change Research. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria, South Africa, pp. 103-118.

 PDF - Published Version Restricted to Repository staff only

Official URL: http://www.sanbi.org/


South Africa is a signatory to several international conventions that address global change and its impacts on biological diversity. Biological invasions are cited as one of the major agents of global change and biological diversity loss and are also a direct cause of the loss of biodiversity in South Africa. South Africa has an active research community that addresses global change in a broad context, including climate change, atmospheric change, land-cover and land-use change, and biological invasions. This chapter reviews the South African Global Change research effort with particular reference to biological invasions. It is concluded that South Africa is well placed to make significant contributions to global research efforts on biological invasions and related global change issues. The chapter also highlights some of the issues that need to be addressed by future research programmes.

13/08/2018

ADIS ABABA, Ethiopia – In the highlands of Ethiopia, where most of the nation’s food is grown, a new approach to farming has helped the country increase its production of chickpeas, an important source of protein for the country’s poor.

English text:
The platform is a forum for farmers to share information on agricultural practices, market prices, and other relevant issues. It has been operational for several years and has helped many farmers improve their productivity and income. However, the platform is currently facing financial challenges, and there is a risk that it may collapse if these challenges are not addressed. Researchers and government officials have expressed concern about the potential impact of the platform’s collapse on the agricultural sector in Ethiopia. They have called for urgent action to address the financial challenges facing the platform and ensure its sustainability. One of the key recommendations made by the researchers and government officials is that the Ministry of Agriculture should provide financial support to the platform. They also recommended that the platform should diversify its sources of income, such as by offering paid services or seeking partnerships with other organizations. Overall, the collapse of the platform would be a significant setback for the agricultural sector in Ethiopia, and it is essential that all stakeholders work together to prevent this from happening.

The spike protein is the key to the virus’s success. It is the first part of the virus that human immune cells encounter, and it is the part that the virus uses to latch onto human cells. The spike protein is also the part of the virus that most vaccines target. So, any changes in the spike protein that help the virus evade the immune system or latch onto human cells more effectively could be very significant.
The spike protein is made up of two main parts: the S1 subunit, which contains the receptor-binding domain (RBD), and the S2 subunit, which helps the spike protein fuse with the human cell membrane. The RBD is the part of the spike protein that binds to the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor on human cells. The S2 subunit is the part of the spike protein that helps the virus enter the cell.
The most significant change in the spike protein of A.23.1 is a deletion in the S1 subunit that removes a small loop of amino acids that is present in the spike protein of other lineages. This deletion is also present in the spike protein of B.1.1.529 (Omicron) variant. The deletion is located in a part of the spike protein that is not directly involved in binding to the ACE2 receptor, but it may still affect the way the spike protein interacts with the immune system.
Another change in the spike protein of A.23.1 is a substitution of a serine amino acid for a proline amino acid at position 988 in the S2 subunit. This substitution is also present in the spike protein of B.1.1.529 (Omicron) variant. The substitution is located in a part of the spike protein that is involved in fusion with the human cell membrane.
The substitution of serine for proline at position 988 in the S2 subunit of the spike protein may affect the way the spike protein interacts with the human cell membrane. It may also affect the way the spike protein is recognized by the immune system.
The convergence of A.23.1 on the same set of proteins as the VOC suggests that these changes in the spike protein may be important for the virus’s ability to evade the immune system and infect human cells. However, more research is needed to understand the significance of these changes.

samples.hyp:
Case Studies Documenting The Reasons for and Circumstances of Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting in Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya
English
Case Studies Documenting The Reasons for and Circumstances of Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting in Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya
12 pages
Abstract

Female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) is a harmful practice that violates the human rights of girls and women. It is defined as all procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. FGM/C is unnecessary and causes immediate and long-term physical and psychological complications. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 200 million girls and women worldwide are currently living with the consequences of FGM/C. The practice is also expected to affect another 68 million girls under the age of 15. FGM/C is concentrated in 30 countries in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. However, the practice is also found in other countries, including the United States. The United Nations (UN) has called for the elimination of FGM/C, and has designated October 9th of each year as the International Day of the Girl Child to raise awareness about the harmful effects of FGM/C. The UN has also designated 2020 as the International Year of the Nurse and the Midwife to recognize the important role of nurses and midwives in addressing the issue of FGM/C. Despite the efforts of the UN and other organizations, FGM/C continues to be practiced in many parts of the world. This paper will examine the reasons for and circumstances of FGM/C in Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya. It will also explore the role of nurses and midwives in addressing the issue of FGM/C in these countries.

samples.src: The floristic composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia in general, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention.
samples.ref: Tsarin nazarin furanni na lambunan gida a arewa-maso-yammacin Habasha gabaɗaya, musamman gundumar Gozamin, ya sami ƙarancin kulawa.
samples.hyp:
English:
The floristic composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia in general, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention. The present study was conducted to assess the floristic diversity, endemism, and conservation value of homegardens in the Gozamin district. A total of 215 homegardens in the district were surveyed, and 1,503 plant species belonging to 134 families and 435 genera were recorded. The families with the highest number of species were Rubiaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae, and Asteraceae. The homegardens exhibited high species diversity and evenness, with a Shannon diversity index of 3.79 and Pielou’s evenness index of 0.83. The study identified 246 endemic and rare species, including 35 forest species, 16 rangeland species, and 195 cultivated species. The homegardens were found to have high conservation value, as they harbor a significant proportion of endemic and rare species. The study highlights the need for further research on the floristic composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia, and the importance of conserving these valuable ecosystems.
Hausa:
Takaitaccen tsarin shuke-shuke a gonakin gida a Arewa maso Yammacin Habasha gaba ɗaya, da kuma yankin Gozamin musamman, ba su samu kulawa sosai daga masu bincike ba. Binciken da aka gudanar a yanzu an yi shi ne don tantance bambancin shuke-shuke, asalin wurin, da kuma muhimmancin kiyayewa na gonakin gida a yankin Gozamin. An gudanar da bincike a gonakin gida guda 215 a yankin, kuma an rubuta nau’o’in shuke-shuke 1,503 daga iyalai 134 da kuma jinsuna 435.
